newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK unemployment to fall again in May.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK unemployment to fall again in May.

text.p: Britain's jobless queues are expected to have shrunk for the 15th month in a row in May while average earnings growth is forecast to have held steady at 4.5 percent.
A Reuters poll of economists produced a consensus forecast for a 40,000 drop in unemployment last month, following a fall of 59,400 in April.
April average earnings are tipped to have grown an annualised 4.5 percent, the same as in March.
Analysts said the jobless figures were somewhat difficult to read given the distorting effects of the jobseekers' allowance, although the underlying growth in job creation is healthy.

"We're fairly optimistic about growth," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers. "So although we reckon the effects of the jobseekers allowance is beginning to wane, it's not going to push the numbers back to the small falls of 10-15,000 we saw before the allowance kicked in."
He is looking for a 45,000 drop in the number of jobless last month.

The allowance was introduced last year and tightened the rules covering eligibility for unemployment benefit. The switch to a new system caused a huge backlog of claims which went unprocessed, artificially inflating the headline jobless figures.
The previous Conservative government claimed a crackdown on fraudulent benefit claims had also pushed the official total lower.

Nonetheless, Salomon Brothers UK economist Michael Saunders thinks falls in unemployment will continue on a sharp downtrend in coming months, forecasting a fall of 50,000 during May, boosted in part by strong job creation.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, agreed.

"With the distortion of the jobseekers' allowance fading, the downward trend in unemployment is likely to have slowed during May," he said. "However, with vacancies at job centres still expanding and service industries reporting increasing recruitment difficulties, there can be little doubt that the labour market is tightening."
Saunders backed the consensus for annualised average earnings growth of 4.5 percent in April. But he thinks May's level will sink as the effect of city bonuses dies out.

"Earnings growth is likely to dip again to 4.25 percent in the next month or two as the effect fades of the high first-quarter bonuses," he said. The third key part of the jobs release covers unit wage costs. The Reuters poll found economists expecting wage costs to have risen 2.5 percent in the three months to April, down from 2.6 the month before.
"The growth of manufacturing unit labour costs continued along its recent downward trend in March and the decline...could continue in April," said Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
